title: Synthesizable sense amps built only from standard logic cells
idea: Paradox: a purely digital cell library performs analog sensing. A 10-person fabless team ships a memory compiler whose sense amps are clock-gated cross-coupled standard-cell inverters, whose decoders and timing are synthesized RTL, and where only the bitcell is hand-drawn; place-and-route pitch-matches the columns, so gain-cell/eDRAM macros port to any logic node via foundry MPW in weeks.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: cuts periphery design NRE ~10x and lets any U.S. logic foundry offer DRAM-class macros, accepting ~20% larger periphery for portability.

title: Store the opposite: cell-polarity-aware row inversion in the controller
idea: Paradox: writing the inverse of the data keeps the data safer. A small team's FPGA/ASIC controller maps each commodity DRAM's true-cell vs anti-cell regions once with a short refresh-paused decay test, then XOR-inverts each row so the dominant value (zeros in sparse/AI data) is stored as the discharged state, keeping a 1-bit polarity tag per row in controller SRAM.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and row hammer (fact 9): only charged cells can leak or be hammered into flipping, so cutting charged cells from ~50% to ~10-20% removes ~3x of flip-prone bits, letting cheaper low-bin dies meet spec.

title: One array's sense amps directly drive another array's wordlines
idea: Paradox: data becomes the address. Two gain-cell macros are abutted at 90 degrees so array A's row-buffer outputs, through compact level shifters, are array B's wordlines; writing a one-hot or multi-hot word into A selects rows of B, deleting B's row decoder and allowing pointer-indirect access in one step. Built in standard CMOS on an MPW by a small fabless team.
why: Periphery (fact 7): removes B's row decoder (~10-15% of macro area) and turns gather/indirection into a single access, cutting controller round trips (data movement, fact 5).

title: Leakage-reset decoders: waste current becomes the precharge clock
idea: Paradox: leakage, normally the enemy, does the resetting. Dynamic row and column decoder nodes are restored by deliberately leaky minimum-length keeper devices with a ~1-2 ns time constant instead of clocked precharge transistors and their clock tree; evaluate pulses are short enough to win against the leak. Implementable by a small fabless team in a standard logic process.
why: Periphery (fact 7): drops precharge devices and clock routing for ~20-30% smaller and ~30% lower-energy decoders in logic-process DRAM-class macros.

title: Stacked fragile core transistors hold full wordline voltage
idea: Paradox: weak devices in series become robust. Wordline drivers in a logic-process DRAM-class macro use two or three stacked thin-oxide core transistors whose middle nodes are dynamically biased so no device ever sees more than VDD, giving ~2-2.5 V wordlines without thick-oxide drivers or level-shifter ladders; a small team can tape it out on any logic MPW.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10) and periphery: thin-oxide stacks are ~2-3x smaller than thick-oxide drivers at equal drive, shrinking wordline driver stripes ~40% and enabling boosted-wordline gain cells in pure core devices.

title: Via-programmed periphery: one frozen base wafer, many memory products
idea: Paradox: a frozen design that stays flexible. A small team tapes out one base wafer whose periphery is a sea-of-gates fabric beside the arrays; just two via masks personalize interface (LPDDR-like, SRAM-like, wide-I/O, CXL-lite), bank count and page size, so a new memory product costs a via-mask set instead of a full tape-out.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): per-variant mask cost drops ~80-90% and time-to-product to ~6 weeks, letting a 10-person team serve many niches from one inventory of base wafers.

title: Unidirectional gridded periphery generator strips EUV from periphery layers
idea: Paradox: taking away design freedom makes the chip cheaper. A small-team EDA generator re-lays all periphery (sense amps, decoders, drivers) on unidirectional gridded tracks with cut masks, so every periphery layer prints with DUV self-aligned multi-patterning on the array's own spacer pitch.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): removes ~2-3 EUV exposures forced by irregular periphery shapes and eases OPC, cutting ~5-8% wafer cost; the product is software a 10-person team can build.

title: Coarse package copper carries the die's fine global buses
idea: Paradox: the crude package does the precise wiring. Global data buses and the power grid of a logic-process DRAM-class chiplet are moved off the die's top metals into a two-layer fan-out RDL formed by an OSAT, landing on micro-pads at each bank edge, so the die needs ~2 fewer metal layers.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4) and data movement (fact 5): thick RDL cuts global-bus RC and IR drop (~3x lower resistance) and removes two metal levels (~8-10% wafer cost), all buyable by a small team as OSAT services.

title: Back-gate cross-coupled sense latch resolves at half-volt arrays
idea: Paradox: the transistor's floor votes on its own decision. In an FD-SOI sense latch built by a small team on a 22 nm MPW, each latch device sits in its own small isolated well whose back gate is wired to the opposite output node, so back gates reinforce regeneration (no trimming), roughly doubling loop gain and letting the latch resolve with ~0.5-0.6 V array voltage.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): dropping array voltage from ~1.0 to ~0.55 V cuts bitline CV2 energy ~3x, at the cost of well-isolation area in the SA stripe.

title: SRAM and gain-cell rows share one column of periphery
idea: Paradox: static and dynamic memory in the same column. A small-team logic-process macro puts a few SRAM rows and many gain-cell rows on one merged single-ended read bitline and one set of sense/write circuits; the SRAM rows act as an in-column cache that gain-cell rows copy into via the shared bitline.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and data movement (fact 5): one periphery serves both densities, ~25% less periphery than separate macros, with an SRAM-speed cache that hides gain-cell latency.

title: Per-mat back-bias flips cells between leaky-fast and tight-slow
idea: Paradox: the same transistor is leaky and fast, then tight and slow. In an FD-SOI gain-cell macro, small per-mat back-gate drivers forward-bias only the mat being accessed and strongly reverse-bias all idle mats, switching in nanoseconds because FD-SOI wells are small; a 10-person team can build it on a 22 nm MPW.
why: Leakage forcing refresh (fact 3): idle-mat off-current drops ~10-100x, giving ~10x longer retention and far less refresh while keeping full access speed.

title: Wave-pipelined decoders keep several addresses in flight without registers
idea: Paradox: a pipeline with no pipeline registers. Decoder trees in a small-team DRAM-class macro are delay-balanced so 2-3 successive addresses travel through them as separate waves at once, sampled only at the wordline drivers, raising the command rate without latch area.
why: Periphery (fact 7): ~2x bank command rate (more bandwidth per mm2 of periphery) with no pipeline-latch overhead; buildable in standard CMOS.

title: Randomly jittered sense-amp firing flattens supply current peaks
idea: Paradox: randomness makes the supply quieter. In a small-team DRAM-class macro, sense-amp groups fire at pseudo-random offsets inside a ~1 ns window chosen per activation from delay codes, spreading the di/dt of thousands of latches so the on-die grid and decap see ~4x lower peak current.
why: Periphery (fact 7): decap and supply-grid area sized for peak current shrink ~40-50%, and lower supply bounce returns ~10-20 mV of sense margin.

title: Bitlines keep rows open after sense amps power down
idea: Paradox: forget in order to remember. After restore the sense latches of a small-team gain-cell macro are powered down and the full-swing bitlines are left floating as a passive copy of the row for ~1 us; later column reads re-sense that strong copy with tiny unbiased inverters, so each bank keeps 4-8 subarray rows 'open' at once.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): ~1.5x higher row-hit rate means fewer activations (energy and row hammer) and no static SA power for open rows.

title: Margin-graded refurbishment turns retired server DIMMs into new supply
idea: Paradox: the used part becomes new supply. A 10-person company runs decommissioned hyperscaler DIMMs (4-6 years old) through FPGA testers that sweep tRCD, VPP and sense-margin corners per rank to estimate remaining margin, then regrades, re-SPDs and resells them for edge servers and CXL capacity tiers.
why: Cost per bit and supply: recovers a large stock of working DRAM otherwise shredded, potentially adding ~10% effective supply at a fraction of new-die cost with no fab.

title: Power rails double as command broadcast wires inside the chip
idea: Paradox: power is data. In a small-team DRAM-class chiplet, mode and command bits are superimposed as ~20-50 mV coded pulses on a local supply rail and recovered by a tiny demodulator in each mat, removing global command and control wires that cross the banks.
why: Periphery routing (fact 7): deletes ~10-20 global control tracks per bank, ~3-5% periphery area, at the cost of supply-noise budgeting.

title: DLL-failed dies salvaged as slow, striped CXL capacity
idea: Paradox: dies with broken periphery become product. DRAM dies that fail high-speed I/O or DLL at sort but have good arrays are packaged and run in DLL-off low-frequency mode behind a small team's CXL controller that stripes each access across many slow dies to restore bandwidth.
why: Cost per bit and supply: periphery-speed yield loss (a few % of output) is turned into sellable capacity at scrap cost, built from bought dies, OSAT packaging and an FPGA/ASIC controller.

title: Read-relocation: every read writes the row somewhere faster
idea: Paradox: every read is a write somewhere else. In a small-team gain-cell macro, after row A is sensed the latch writes it into a free row in the short-bitline fast segment next to the sense amps instead of restoring A, and a small per-bank remap table tracks it log-structured style; hot rows migrate there automatically and aggressor rows never stay put.
why: Latency/energy and row hammer (fact 9): ~70-80% of accesses land in the fast segment and repeated activation of one physical row is diluted, with no separate migration engine.

title: Sense-amp latches chained into an in-situ pattern generator
idea: Paradox: the memory's own latches invent its test data. In test mode, adjacent sense latches of a small-team DRAM-class macro are chained through XOR taps into a row-wide LFSR that writes pseudo-random patterns row by row and compacts read-back signatures in place, removing the BIST pattern generator, comparators and test I/O.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and test cost: test logic area ~-50% and test time ~5x shorter through full-row parallelism.

title: Periphery placed inside TSV keep-out zones by stress-aware design
idea: Paradox: zones forbidden to transistors host transistors. In a small team's 3D-stacked DRAM-class chiplets (foundry TSV service), stress-tolerant periphery (long-channel digital decoders, pumps, decap, ESD) is placed inside TSV keep-out rings with channels oriented along the low-piezoresistance direction, while matched analog stays outside.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims ~3-6% of die area lost to keep-out zones, lowering wafer area per stacked bit.

title: CMP dummy metal fill rewired as functional decoupling capacitance
idea: Paradox: filler that exists only for polishing becomes a circuit. A small-team EDA step replaces floating metal-fill tiles in periphery regions with interdigitated VDD/VSS comb fill on alternating layers, forming metal-oxide-metal decap that still meets density rules and replaces dedicated MOS decap cells.
why: Periphery (fact 7): MOS decap is ~5-10% of periphery area; recovering it from fill yields ~2-4% die area at no process cost.
